newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Aznar highlights economy on anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar highlights economy on anniversary.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar boasted of his government's successful management of the economy on Monday, the first anniversary of its coming to power, but a bombing by Basque separatists served as a reminder of a 29-year conflict he has failed to resolve.

Hours before Aznar met members of his centre-right Popular Party to give an account of the year's accomplishments, two bombs exploded at a military base near the Basque regional capital of Vitoria, causing heavy property damage but no injuries.

"More people are employed than were one year ago, electricity and telephones are cheaper, investments are profitable and solid, stable, durable growth is expected," Aznar told his party's executive committee.

The 44-year-old former tax attorney came to power last year after 13 years of Socialist rule. Since then, he has imposed a strict austerity programme, bringing inflation to a 29-year low of 2.2 percent in March while slashing public spending.
Liberalisation and privatisation have increased competition and cut electricity and phone costs while financial markets have demonstrated confidence in the economy with hefty gains.
The achievements have won newfound respect for Spain's once-chaotic economy.
Aznar is now confident the dramatic strides on the economic front will win Spain a place among the founders of a single European currency set to be launched in 1999.
It is in the political realm that the conservative ruling party, which traces its roots to the four-decade dictatorship of Francisco Franco, has come in for most public criticism.

There has been no progress toward resolving the conflict with ETA which has intensified its guerilla campaign this year after a relative lull in 1996. ETA, which stands for Basque Homeland and Freedom, has killed nine people so far this year, two of them in the past two weeks.
The group has killed about 800 people in almost three decades of struggle for an independent state encompassing parts of northern Spain and southern France.
The government has repeatedly ruled out any peace talks with ETA unless it renounces violence first.
"The conditions for dialogue are not right and the objectives of this presumed dialogue are not set," Aznar said in an interview with the daily El Mundo published on Monday.

While most Spaniards are apparently pleased with economic progress, polls show many do not like the government's new hard line policy against Cuba which has prompted several diplomatic incidents with Havana.

They were also unhappy about a government decision last August to keep secret key documents on a 1980s "dirty war" against ETA, which implicated the former Socialist government in a series of kidnappings and killings from 1983-1987. It was a slap in the face to Aznar when the Supreme Court overturned that decision in March.
